'''Sallie P. Mead''' (born '''Sallie Eugena Pero''', October 1, 1893 – April 1981) was an American mathematician and engineer known for her contributions to [[Radar|radar technology]] and the development of [[Waveguide (radio frequency)|waveguides]] at the [[American Telephone and Telegraph Company]]'s development and research arm (AT&T D&R).

== Early life ==
Sallie P. Mead was born on October 1, 1893, in Manhattan, New York, to Robert R. Pero and Lillian M. Foggin. She began studying at [[Barnard College]] in 1909 and graduated in 1913, earning the highest honors in mathematics and winning the Barnard's Kohn Mathematical Prize. She continued her studies at [[Columbia University]], where she earned a master's degree in mathematics. Her master's essay, titled "Linear Transformations and the Theory of the Tetrahedron" focused on the application of [[Linear map|linear transformations]] and the [[Tetrahedral symmetry|rotation group of the tetrahedron]] to the solution of general [[quartic equation]]s.

== Career ==
Mead received a license to teach mathematics as a substitute in New York City schools, with her first assignment at [[Evander Childs Educational Campus|Evander Childs High School]] in the Bronx. By June 1915, she had joined AT&T's Western Union building on Broadway, hired by [[George Ashley Campbell]] as a "[[Computer (occupation)|computer]]" to work on transmission probability problems.<ref name="Coxson2022">{{cite web
| last1 = Coxson
| first1 = Gregory
| last2 = Haloupek
| first2 = William
| title = Sallie P. Mead: An Industrial Mathematician in the Early 20th Century
| website = Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics
| date = 2022-06-15
| url = https://sinews.siam.org/Details-Page/sallie-p-mead-an-industrial-mathematician-in-the-early-20th-century
| access-date = 2024-05-19
}}</ref> In 1923, Campbell credited Mead in a technical paper for her meticulous work on the exponential [[Poisson distribution]].<ref>
{{cite journal
 | last = Brittain
 | first = J. E.
 | title = Electrical Engineering Hall of Fame: George C. Southworth [Scanning Our Past]
 | journal = Proceedings of the IEEE
 | volume = 98
 | issue = 10
 | pages = 1787–1790
 | date = October 2010
 | doi = 10.1109/JPROC.2010.2060249
}}
</ref>

=== Transition to engineer ===
In 1919, Pero transitioned from "computer" to "engineer" at AT&T D&R's Transmission Engineering unit under supervisor [[John Renshaw Carson]]. Mead developed expertise in the mathematics of transmission through cables, wires, and conducting tubes, especially those with circular cross sections. In 1924, she applied for a patent on a "distortion compensator," becoming the first woman at AT&T to hold a patent upon its granting in 1929.<ref name = firstPatent>
{{cite patent
 | country = US
 | number = 1709037
 | title = Distortion compensator
 | status = patent
 | url
 | inventor = Sallie E. Pero
 | gdate = 1929-04-16
 | url = https://patents.google.com/patent/US1709037A/en?oq=1709037
}}
</ref> Mead earned six patents throughout her career. She became the first woman to publish in the ''[[Bell Labs Technical Journal|Bell System Technical Journal]]'' and went on to author six ''BSTJ'' articles.<ref name = Coxson2022/>

=== Contributions to waveguide development ===
In the early 1930s, Mead was assigned as an analyst to provide mathematical support to [[George Southworth]]'s development of waveguides, crucial for [[Microwave|microwave radar technology]] in World War II.
<ref name="Coxson2024">{{cite conference
|last1 = Coxson
|first1 = Gregory
|last2 = Haloupek
|first2 = William
|title = How Two Industrial Mathematicians at AT&T Helped Spur Waveguide Research in the 1930s
|book-title = Proceceedings of the 2024 IEEE Conference on Radar
|year = 2024
|location = Denver, CO
}}</ref>
Along with [[Sergei Schelkunoff]], Mead rediscovered [[John William Strutt, 3rd Baron Rayleigh|Lord Rayleigh]]'s findings on waveguide cutoff frequencies, and their work went on to extend Rayleigh's results to include metal attenuation losses.{{Sfnp|Carson|Mead|Schelkunoff|1936}}
Southworth himself was unsure which of the two was first to describe the effect.<ref name = "Southworth1962">{{cite book
| last1 = Southworth
| first1 = George C.
| title = Forty Years of Radio Research: A Reportorial Account
| publisher = Gordon and Breach Science Publishers, Inc.
| year = 1962
| location = New York, NY
| url = https://archive.org/details/fortyyearsofradi00sout/page/n3/mode/2up
| page = [https://archive.org/details/fortyyearsofradi00sout/page/134/mode/2up?q=mead 135]
}}</ref> The work of Mead and Shelkunoff on the attenuation of the [[Transverse mode|TE01 mode]] led to significant advancements in microwave communications. Mead retired in 1958, remarking that she looked forward to having more time study mathematics and Russian.<ref name = "Coxson2022"/>

== Personal life ==
Mead married Charles Edwin Mead in 1924, who died in 1934. She married Chester E. Grant in 1938 but continued to use the name Sallie P. Mead professionally.<ref name = "Coxson2022"/>

== Later years and legacy ==
During World War II, Mead contributed to the development of [[fire-control system]]s. Post-war, she conducted probabilistic studies of communication traffic in the Traffic Department until her retirement in 1958. Mead died in April 1981 in New Jersey.<ref name = "Coxson2022"/>

== Awards and honors ==
* Barnard's Kohn Mathematical Prize (1913)
* First woman at AT&T to hold a patent (1929)<ref name = "firstPatent"/>
* Member of the American Mathematical Society (1923)<ref name = "Coxson2024"/>
